blocks.body:
Every course in algebra or topology builds the same constructions again and again. The product of two groups, of two vector spaces and of two topological spaces are each defined separately, yet in each case the product is the thing with two projection maps through which every pair of maps factors uniquely. A finite-dimensional vector space is isomorphic to its dual and to its double dual, yet every textbook insists that the second isomorphism is "natural" and the first is not. What do these words mean?

Category theory gives the precise language. Its basic idea is to study objects through the maps between them. A category records objects and maps, a functor is a map between categories, and a natural transformation is a map between functors; with these, "natural" becomes a definition. The examples come from [[groups]], [[vector-spaces]] and [[topological-spaces]].

blocks.title: Category
Examples of categories
blocks.body:
The familiar categories have structured sets as objects and structure-preserving functions as morphisms: $\mathbf{Set}$ (sets and all functions), $\mathbf{Grp}$ (groups and homomorphisms), $\mathbf{Vect}_k$ (vector spaces over $k$ and linear maps), $\mathbf{Top}$ (topological spaces and continuous maps). In each, composition is composition of functions, which is automatically associative.

But morphisms need not be functions, and some of the most useful small examples look nothing like these.

- A partially ordered set $(P, \le)$ is a category: the objects are the elements, and there is exactly one morphism $x \to y$ when $x \le y$ and none otherwise. Reflexivity gives identities and transitivity gives composition.
- A group $G$ is a category with a single object $\ast$, whose morphisms $\ast \to \ast$ are the elements of $G$ and whose composition is the group operation. In this category every morphism is an isomorphism.
- The matrix category over a field $k$ has the natural numbers $0, 1, 2, \dots$ as objects, $m \times n$ matrices as the morphisms $n \to m$, and matrix multiplication as composition; the identity matrix $I_n$ is $\mathrm{id}_n$.

Because a category is described entirely by arrows, a definition that uses only arrows makes sense in every category at once. For example, a product of $X$ and $Y$ is an object $P$ with morphisms $p_1\colon P \to X$, $p_2\colon P \to Y$ such that for every pair $f\colon T \to X$, $g\colon T \to Y$ there is exactly one $h\colon T \to P$ with $p_1 \circ h = f$ and $p_2 \circ h = g$. In $\mathbf{Set}$, $\mathbf{Grp}$, $\mathbf{Vect}_k$ and $\mathbf{Top}$ this produces the Cartesian product, the direct product, the direct sum and the product topology. In a poset it produces the greatest lower bound. Any two products of $X$ and $Y$ are isomorphic by a unique isomorphism compatible with the projections, which is why one says "the" product.

blocks.title: Functor
blocks.body:
A (covariant) functor $F\colon \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}$ assigns to each object $X$ of $\mathcal{C}$ an object $F(X)$ of $\mathcal{D}$, and to each morphism $f\colon X \to Y$ a morphism $F(f)\colon F(X) \to F(Y)$, such that
$$F(g \circ f) = F(g) \circ F(f), \qquad F(\mathrm{id}_X) = \mathrm{id}_{F(X)}.$$
A contravariant functor is the same except that it reverses arrows: $F(f)\colon F(Y) \to F(X)$ and $F(g \circ f) = F(f) \circ F(g)$.

A functor is a construction that applies not only to objects but also to maps, compatibly with composition.

blocks.title: Examples of functors
blocks.body:
- Forgetful functors, such as $U\colon \mathbf{Grp} \to \mathbf{Set}$, send a group to its underlying set and a homomorphism to the same function.
- The free vector space functor $\mathbf{Set} \to \mathbf{Vect}_k$ sends a set $S$ to the space with basis $S$, and a function to the linear map that does the same thing to basis vectors.
- Abelianisation $G \mapsto G^{\mathrm{ab}} = G/[G,G]$ is a functor $\mathbf{Grp} \to \mathbf{Grp}$: a homomorphism $\varphi\colon G \to H$ maps commutators to commutators, so it induces $G^{\mathrm{ab}} \to H^{\mathrm{ab}}$.
- The dual space $V \mapsto V^* = \mathrm{Hom}(V, k)$ is contravariant: a linear map $f\colon V \to W$ induces $f^*\colon W^* \to V^*$, $f^*(\psi) = \psi \circ f$, and $(g \circ f)^* = f^* \circ g^*$.
- For a fixed object $A$, the hom functor $\mathrm{Hom}(A, -)\colon \mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{Set}$ sends $X$ to $\mathrm{Hom}(A, X)$ and $f\colon X \to Y$ to the function $u \mapsto f \circ u$.
- The fundamental group sends a pointed space $(X, x_0)$ to the group $\pi_1(X, x_0)$ and a continuous pointed map to the induced homomorphism of loops; see [[fundamental-group]]. Homology groups are functors in the same way; see [[homology]].
- A functor from a group regarded as a one-object category to $\mathbf{Vect}_k$ is exactly a representation of the group; see [[group-representations]].

The first payoff of the definition costs one line.

blocks.title: Functors preserve isomorphisms
blocks.body: Every functor sends isomorphisms to isomorphisms. Consequently, if $F(X)$ and $F(Y)$ are not isomorphic, then $X$ and $Y$ are not isomorphic.

If $g \circ f = \mathrm{id}_X$ and $f \circ g = \mathrm{id}_Y$, then $F(g) \circ F(f) = F(g \circ f) = F(\mathrm{id}_X) = \mathrm{id}_{F(X)}$, and likewise $F(f) \circ F(g) = \mathrm{id}_{F(Y)}$. (For a contravariant functor the same computation works with the order reversed.)

blocks.title: Natural transformation
blocks.body:
Let $F, G\colon \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}$ be functors. A natural transformation $\eta\colon F \Rightarrow G$ is a family of morphisms $\eta_X\colon F(X) \to G(X)$ in $\mathcal{D}$, one for each object $X$ of $\mathcal{C}$, such that for every morphism $f\colon X \to Y$
$$\eta_Y \circ F(f) = G(f) \circ \eta_X .$$
It is a natural isomorphism if every component $\eta_X$ is an isomorphism.

The condition (often drawn as a commuting square) says that $\eta$ is given by one uniform rule that does not depend on arbitrary choices made separately for each object: transporting along $f$ and then applying $\eta$ gives the same result as applying $\eta$ and then transporting.

blocks.title: Example 1: the double dual is natural
blocks.body: For a vector space $V$ over $k$, let $\mathrm{ev}_V\colon V \to V^{**}$ be evaluation, $\mathrm{ev}_V(v)(\varphi) = \varphi(v)$. Show that $\mathrm{ev}$ is a natural transformation from the identity functor to the double dual functor $V \mapsto V^{**}$ (which is covariant, being contravariant twice).
blocks.solution:
Let $f\colon V \to W$ be linear. The double dual functor sends it to $f^{**}\colon V^{**} \to W^{**}$, $f^{**}(\Theta) = \Theta \circ f^*$. We must check $\mathrm{ev}_W \circ f = f^{**} \circ \mathrm{ev}_V$. Apply both sides to $v \in V$ and then to $\psi \in W^*$:
$$\big(f^{**}(\mathrm{ev}_V(v))\big)(\psi) = \mathrm{ev}_V(v)\big(f^*\psi\big) = (\psi \circ f)(v) = \psi(f(v)) = \mathrm{ev}_W(f(v))(\psi).$$
So the square commutes for every $f$. No basis was used. For finite-dimensional $V$ each $\mathrm{ev}_V$ is injective (a nonzero $v$ extends to a basis, and the coordinate functional of $v$ does not vanish on it) between spaces of equal dimension, hence an isomorphism. So, on finite-dimensional spaces, $\mathrm{ev}$ is a natural isomorphism; see [[dual-spaces]].

blocks.title: Example 2: the dual is not naturally isomorphic
blocks.body: A finite-dimensional space is also isomorphic to its dual $V^*$, by sending a basis to the dual basis. Show that no such isomorphism can be chosen naturally, even if we only ask for compatibility with invertible maps. Precisely: work over $\mathbb{Q}$ and suppose that for each finite-dimensional $V$ we have an isomorphism $\eta_V\colon V \to V^*$ with $f^* \circ \eta_W \circ f = \eta_V$ for every invertible linear $f\colon V \to W$. Derive a contradiction.
blocks.solution:
(The condition $f^* \circ \eta_W \circ f = \eta_V$ is the natural form of the requirement, since $V \mapsto V^*$ reverses arrows.) Take $V = W = \mathbb{Q}$ and $f$ = multiplication by $2$. A linear map $\eta\colon \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{Q}^*$ has the form $\eta(v)(w) = a v w$ for a fixed scalar $a$, and it is an isomorphism exactly when $a \ne 0$.

Compute the left-hand side: $(f^* \circ \eta \circ f)(v)$ is the functional $w \mapsto \eta(f v)(f w) = a (2v)(2w) = 4 a v w$. The condition demands $4a = a$, so $a = 0$, and $\eta_{\mathbb{Q}}$ is not an isomorphism. Contradiction.

So every isomorphism $V \cong V^*$ depends on a choice (a basis, or an inner product), whereas $V \cong V^{**}$ does not.

blocks.title: Yoneda lemma
blocks.body:
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a category, $A$ an object, and $F\colon \mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{Set}$ a functor. The map
$$\mathrm{Nat}\big(\mathrm{Hom}(A, -), F\big) \to F(A), \qquad \eta \mapsto \eta_A(\mathrm{id}_A)$$
is a bijection. Its inverse sends $x \in F(A)$ to the transformation with components $\eta_X(u) = F(u)(x)$ for $u\colon A \to X$.

Given $x \in F(A)$, define $\eta^x_X(u) = F(u)(x)$. This is natural: for $f\colon X \to Y$ and $u \in \mathrm{Hom}(A, X)$,
$$\eta^x_Y(f \circ u) = F(f \circ u)(x) = F(f)\big(F(u)(x)\big) = F(f)\big(\eta^x_X(u)\big).$$
And $\eta^x_A(\mathrm{id}_A) = F(\mathrm{id}_A)(x) = x$, so $x \mapsto \eta^x$ followed by $\eta \mapsto \eta_A(\mathrm{id}_A)$ is the identity.

Conversely let $\eta$ be any natural transformation and $x = \eta_A(\mathrm{id}_A)$. For $u\colon A \to X$, naturality applied to the morphism $u$ and the element $\mathrm{id}_A$ gives
$$\eta_X(u) = \eta_X(u \circ \mathrm{id}_A) = F(u)\big(\eta_A(\mathrm{id}_A)\big) = F(u)(x) = \eta^x_X(u).$$
So $\eta = \eta^x$, and the two maps are mutually inverse.

blocks.title: What the Yoneda lemma means, and adjunctions
blocks.body:
The Yoneda lemma says that a natural transformation out of $\mathrm{Hom}(A, -)$ is completely determined by where it sends the single element $\mathrm{id}_A$. Taking $F = \mathrm{Hom}(B, -)$, one deduces that natural transformations $\mathrm{Hom}(A,-) \Rightarrow \mathrm{Hom}(B,-)$ correspond to morphisms $B \to A$, and hence that $A \cong B$ as soon as $\mathrm{Hom}(A, -) \cong \mathrm{Hom}(B, -)$ naturally. An object is determined up to isomorphism by the maps out of it. This is the precise form of the slogan at the start, and it is why universal properties (which describe hom sets) determine objects.

A related key notion is adjunction. The free group functor $F\colon \mathbf{Set} \to \mathbf{Grp}$ and the forgetful functor $U$ satisfy
$$\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Grp}}(F(S), G) \cong \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Set}}(S, U(G)),$$
naturally in both $S$ and $G$: a homomorphism out of a free group is the same as an arbitrary function on its generators. One says $F$ is left adjoint to $U$. Free modules, abelianisation, tensor products ([[tensor-products]]) and the Stone–Čech compactification are all adjoints, and a general theorem (stated here without proof) says that left adjoints preserve colimits (such as quotients and direct sums) and right adjoints preserve limits (such as products and kernels).

blocks.title: Example 3: counting functors between posets
blocks.body: Regard the chain $0 < 1 < 2$ as a category $\mathbf{3}$. How many functors $\mathbf{3} \to \mathbf{3}$ are there? How many natural transformations are there from the identity functor to the constant functor at $2$, and from the constant functor at $2$ to the identity?
blocks.solution:
In a poset category there is at most one morphism between two objects. So a functor is determined by its values on objects, $i \mapsto F(i)$, and it exists precisely when every morphism $i \to j$ (that is, every $i \le j$) has somewhere to go, namely $F(i) \le F(j)$. Composition and identities are then preserved automatically, because there is only one possible arrow. Functors between posets are exactly order-preserving maps.

Counting nondecreasing maps $\{0,1,2\} \to \{0,1,2\}$: such a map is determined by how many of the three inputs go to each output, which is a way of writing $3$ as an ordered sum of three nonnegative parts. By stars and bars there are $\binom{3+2}{2} = 10$ of them.

A natural transformation $\eta\colon F \Rightarrow G$ between such functors needs a morphism $F(i) \to G(i)$ for every $i$, i.e. $F(i) \le G(i)$; the naturality squares commute automatically, again because parallel arrows in a poset are equal. From the identity to the constant functor $2$ we need $i \le 2$ for all $i$: exactly one transformation. In the other direction we need $2 \le i$ for all $i$, which fails at $i = 0$: none. So between poset-valued functors there is at most one natural transformation, and it exists iff $F \le G$ pointwise.

blocks.title: Example 4: a functor proves a topological fact
blocks.body: Use the fundamental group functor to show that there is no continuous map $r\colon D^2 \to S^1$ from the closed disc to its boundary circle with $r(z) = z$ for all $z \in S^1$ (a retraction).
blocks.solution:
Let $i\colon S^1 \to D^2$ be the inclusion. A retraction would satisfy $r \circ i = \mathrm{id}_{S^1}$. Apply the functor $\pi_1$ (with base point $1 \in S^1$):
$$\pi_1(r) \circ \pi_1(i) = \pi_1(r \circ i) = \pi_1(\mathrm{id}_{S^1}) = \mathrm{id}_{\pi_1(S^1)}.$$
Now $\pi_1(S^1) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ and $\pi_1(D^2)$ is trivial, since the disc is convex and every loop contracts by straight-line homotopy. So the identity of $\mathbb{Z}$ factors through the trivial group, $\mathbb{Z} \to 1 \to \mathbb{Z}$, which is impossible because such a composite sends $1$ to $0$. This is the core of Brouwer's fixed point theorem in dimension $2$.

blocks.body:
- A functor must act on morphisms, not only on objects, and must respect composition. The centre $G \mapsto Z(G)$ is a perfectly good rule on objects but is not a functor on $\mathbf{Grp}$ (see the exercises).
- Naturality is a property of a whole family, not of each component. Every $V$ is isomorphic to $V^*$; what fails is the existence of a family of such isomorphisms compatible with all maps.
- In a general category, morphisms need not be functions and objects need not have elements, so arguments like "pick $x \in X$" do not make sense in a poset or a one-object category.
- The objects of $\mathbf{Set}$ do not form a set (there is no set of all sets). Categories whose objects form a set are called small; the distinction matters when forming functor categories or applying the Yoneda lemma to large categories.

Functors are the organising principle of algebraic topology: [[fundamental-group]] and [[homology]] are functors from spaces to groups, and their functoriality is what turns computations into impossibility proofs. In algebra, [[tensor-products]] and [[dual-spaces]] are best understood through universal properties and natural isomorphisms, and modules over a ring form a category with kernels and cokernels; see [[modules]]. Representations of a group are functors out of the group regarded as a category; see [[group-representations]]. Taking derivatives at base points is a functor on pointed [[smooth-manifolds|smooth manifolds]], and passing from a Lie group to its Lie algebra is a functor on [[lie-groups|Lie groups]]. In logic and computer science, categories model types and programs, and the internal logic of a category connects with [[logic-basics]].

1. Show that the vertical composite of two natural transformations $F \Rightarrow G \Rightarrow H$ is a natural transformation.
2. Show that the quotient maps $G \to G^{\mathrm{ab}}$ form a natural transformation from the identity functor on $\mathbf{Grp}$ to abelianisation.
3. Let $i\colon \mathbb{Z}/2 \to S_3$ send the generator to a transposition and let $\mathrm{sgn}\colon S_3 \to \mathbb{Z}/2$ be the sign. Use $\mathrm{sgn} \circ i = \mathrm{id}$ and $Z(S_3) = 1$ to show that there is no functor $F\colon \mathbf{Grp} \to \mathbf{Grp}$ with $F(G) = Z(G)$ for every group $G$, however $F$ is defined on morphisms.
4. In a poset regarded as a category, show that the product of $x$ and $y$, when it exists, is their greatest lower bound.
